deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page belongs to Riemann's Naturphilosophie fragments on gravitation and light, the ether-sink hypothesis, which appear in his collected works (Werke, 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts', 'Gravitation und Licht'). On the previous page Riemann proposes that space is filled with a continuous 'Stoff' (ether). This ether streams toward every ponderable point with a speed proportional to that point's attractive power and inversely proportional to the square of the distance. The same quantity of Stoff always occupies the same volume, so the flow is incompressible.

(1) Sink postulate (top of the page). The previous sentence is completed: in every ponderable body, in equal times, equal amounts of Stoff disappear, proportional to the body's gravitational mass. In modern terms, with incompressible ether velocity v:
  div v = -k * sum_i m_i * delta(x - x_i).
For a single point mass, v = -k m r_hat / (4 pi r^2). The step k*m/(4 pi) is my normalisation. This is the hydrodynamic analogue of Poisson's equation, with the ether flow playing the role of the gravitational field.

(2) Well-posedness claim. Riemann asserts that these laws completely determine the motion of the Stoff in any bounded region, given:
  - the positions of all ponderable parts and their gravitational strengths (the sources), and
  - the external forces acting on the boundary points (boundary data).
No proof is given. The dynamical law from the previous page, a 'memory'-type elastic law in which force depends on earlier strains of line and volume elements, is assumed.

(3) Replacing the boundary data by a condition at infinity. If ponderable bodies occupy only a finite part of space (example: neglecting the fixed stars when treating the solar system), then the motion of the Stoff becomes infinitely small at infinite distance, |v| ~ 1/r^2 -> 0.

(4) Approximation by a large domain. Enclose the bodies in a region whose boundary is everywhere very far from them, and force the Stoff outside it to be at rest. The resulting motions approximate the true ones (those needed to explain gravity) arbitrarily well as the boundary recedes. Under this assumption the physical space outside the closed region is unchangeable, i.e. undeformed. This is an exterior-problem / limit-of-bounded-domains argument, as in potential theory.

(5) Section '((Blatt 15))' is purely philosophical; there are no formulas. Particular, i.e. locally bounded, purposiveness requires a cause bounded in time and space. General purposes are explained by an eternal Will not bounded by any temporal process. The only purposiveness whose cause we perceive is that of our own actions, and its cause is our thinking. Hence all perceived purposiveness must be explained by a thought process. This leads into the next page on organisms and Fechner.

The pencil marginalia ('In Blatt 18 enthalten!' and a page/line reference) are editorial cross-references.
errors: No computation is present, so there are no algebraic slips.
The uniqueness and determinacy claim (motion determined by sources plus boundary forces) is asserted without proof. Given Riemann's hereditary, memory-dependent force law, this is a nontrivial claim.

Possible tension in step (4). With sinks absorbing Stoff at a constant rate, the total flux through any enclosing surface is k*sum m_i, independent of the surface's distance. Pointwise velocity tends to 0 like 1/r^2, but the flux does not vanish. Holding the Stoff outside a large boundary strictly at rest is therefore incompatible with incompressibility plus sinks, unless Stoff can cross the boundary or the boundary condition is read as 'undeformed outer space' rather than 'zero velocity'. The final sentence, about the physical space outside being unchangeable, suggests the latter reading. Riemann does not address this point.

results.what: Gravitation explained by incompressible ether flowing into ponderable bodies, which act as sinks of strength proportional to their mass; velocity proportional to m/r^2.
results.modern_name: Ether-sink (fluid-flow) model of gravitation; hydrodynamic analogue of Poisson's equation
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (fragment 'Gravitation und Licht', published posthumously in Werke 1876). Similar sink ideas appear in Euler and later Bjerknes/Challis-type hydrodynamic analogies.

results.what: Motion determined by the sources plus boundary data; boundary data replaced by decay at infinity via approximation with large bounded domains.
results.modern_name: Exterior boundary value problem / domain-exhaustion approximation (radiation or decay condition at infinity)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard in 19th-century potential theory (Green, Gauss, Dirichlet)

results.what: Teleological argument: purposiveness explained by thought processes, with local versus general purposes.
results.modern_name: Riemann's metaphysical fragments (influenced by Herbart and Fechner)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, published in Werke ('Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik')

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known ether-sink theory of gravitation and the teleology passage, both published in Riemann's Werke. The page contains no new mathematics, only qualitative claims about determinacy and the approximation at infinity.

checkable.asserts: Equals 0: the radial inflow v = -r_hat/r^2 is divergence-free away from the sink, so Stoff elements keep their volume.
Equals 4*pi independent of R: the inflow flux through any sphere around the sink is constant, so the velocity decays but the flux at infinity does not.
Equals 0: the motion of the Stoff becomes infinitely small at infinite distance from finitely many ponderable bodies.

transcription_corrections: 'Denkt man daher die ponderabeln Körper in einen Raum eingeschlossen werden' should probably read 'Wenn daher die ponderabeln Körper in einen Raum eingeschlossen werden'. The grammar requires 'wenn', and the image is consistent with it.
'und den Stoff außerhalb desselben gefroren [?] ist, zu ruhen' should likely read 'und der Stoff außerhalb desselben gezwungen ist, zu ruhen'.
The pencil margin note '41 [?] Zeile 9' is an editorial cross-reference; its first characters are uncertain.
